newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Airbus puts pressure on EU over Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: Airbus puts pressure on EU over Boeing merger.

text.p: The European Commission is under increasing pressure to set tough conditions on the merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas after Airbus Industrie, their only big rival, said bluntly that it could not survive if the deal went through.

Ending months of sometimes contradictory and muted statements of concern, Airbus proclaimed forcefully on Saturday its belief that the merger was part of a deliberate U.S. government-led plan to eliminate the European consortium.
"A merger to kill Airbus" was how the French newspaper Le Monde headed an article written by Airbus's managing director Jean Pierson.
The accusation met with an equally strong reaction from Boeing's commercial aircraft head, Ron Woodard, who said Pierson was "totally paranoid".
He added that under Boeing's billion-dollar investment plan to reduce the average time required to build an aircraft to just six months, it would be even harder for Airbus to survive.
"Anyone having a difficult time competing with us now is going to have a horrible time with the new system," Woodward said on Sunday at Paris's Le Bourget air show. "This is going to bury them".
With regulatory probes of the deal on both sides of the Atlantic near an end, the gloves are now clearly off between the two rivals.

Boeing hopes the Federal Trade Commission of the United States will give its views on the $14 billion merger by July 1. If the FTC clears the merger, as the Seattle-based manufacturer seems to believe it will, and the EU executive asks for significant concessions, this could trigger a damaging transatlantic political dispute.
The EU must make a final decision by July 31. But it will submit a draft decision to an advisory committee of national antitrust experts on July 4.

Under EU merger control law, the Commission must probe all mergers or acquisitions involving companies with a worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units and EU sales of 250 million Ecus each irrespective of their nationality.
Boeing acknowledged this by filing the deal for approval in the Union in February.

The 1990 merger law allows the Commission to seek concessions, usually in the form of asset sell-offs, in return for its clearance. But if the companies fail to provide remedies that ensure fair competition, it may block the deal altogether.
Recently it forced South African mining group Anglo American to cut drastically its shareholding in Lonrho Plc to stop it taking control of the British conglomerate.
And In 1991, the Commission banned France's Aerospatiale, a key partner in Airbus, and Alenia of Italy from taking control of Boeing's De Havilland -- the first veto in EU history.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has made it clear that the Boeing merger will not go through as it stands.

He particularly took aim at recent long-term exclusive supply contracts signed with U.S. airlines, AMR's American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and Continental Airlines as reflecting Boeing's strong position.

German Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt also stressed at the Paris airshow on Monday that "the contracts document the great danger that goes out from the increasingly stronger market position of Boeing/MDD".
"Through exclusive contracts American airline companies will be bound to one provider and the American market will be blocked for Airbus," Rexrodt said.
Airbus is a consortium owned by France's Aerospatiale , Daimler-Benz Aerospace, British Aerospace BAe and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas.
Although the exclusive pacts are a significant sticking point, scrapping them would not prevent Boeing from increasing its stronghold on the market.

Boeing currently provides 60 percent of the world's new commercial aircraft. McDonnell Douglas, which makes mainly military planes, only gives it another four percent, but the Commission and Airbus point to the presence of many a DC9 and MD89 in European fleets for which , if the merger was allowed, Boeing would be a 'natural' replacement.
Forcing the companies to sell assets will not be an easy task however, as Boeing and McDonnell do not have any manufacturing assets in Europe, European antitrust experts noted.
They pointed out that it would be legally difficult for the Commission to enforce any conditions outside the EU's territory especially in a deal with such strong defence interests.
"It's all too mixed up with the geographical question of where the deal is and the defence interests it poses," one lawyer said. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
